edits.before: <para id="import-auto-id1169738094619">Yet another quantum number emerges from decay lifetimes and patterns. Note that the particles <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mtext>Λ</m:mtext><m:mtext>,</m:mtext><m:mspace width="0.25em"/><m:mtext>Σ</m:mtext><m:mtext>,</m:mtext><m:mspace width="0.25em"/><m:mtext>Ξ</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{Λ,`Σ,`Ξ} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>, and <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mo stretchy="false">Ω</m:mo></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ %OMEGA } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> decay with lifetimes on the order of <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mn>10</m:mn><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mo stretchy="false">−</m:mo><m:mn>10</m:mn></m:mrow></m:mrow></m:msup></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{"10" rSup { size 8{ - "10"} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> s (the exception is <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mtext>Σ</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mn>0</m:mn></m:mrow></m:msup></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{Σ rSup { size 8{0} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>, whose short lifetime is explained by its particular quark substructure.), implying that their decay is caused by the weak force alone, although they are hadrons and feel the strong force. The decay modes of these particles also show patterns—in particular, certain decays that should be possible within all the known conservation laws do not occur. Whenever something is possible in physics, it will happen. If something does not happen, it is forbidden by a rule. All this seemed strange to those studying these particles when they were first discovered, so they named a new quantum number <term id="import-auto-id1169737981379">strangeness</term>, given the symbol <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>S</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{S} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> in the table given above. The values of strangeness assigned to various particles are based on the decay systematics. It is found that <emphasis>strangeness is conserved by the strong force</emphasis>, which governs the production of most of these particles in accelerator experiments. However, <emphasis>strangeness is <emphasis effect="italics">not conserved</emphasis> by the weak force</emphasis>. This conclusion is reached from the fact that particles that have long lifetimes decay via the weak force and do not conserve strangeness. All of this also has implications for the carrier particles, since they transmit forces and are thus involved in these decays.</para>
edits.after: <para id="import-auto-id1169738094619">Some hadrons are readily produced through strong interactions but decay much more slowly through the weak interaction. This unexpected behavior led physicists to introduce a quantum number called <term id="import-auto-id1169737981379">strangeness</term>, denoted by <m:math><m:mi>S</m:mi></m:math>. Total strangeness is conserved in strong and electromagnetic interactions but can change in weak interactions. Consequently, a decay that changes strangeness must proceed through the weak interaction. These conservation rules helped explain the observed patterns of particle production and decay.</para><para id="strangeness-totalitarian-principle">A memorable maxim associated with Murray Gell-Mann captures the search for such rules: “Everything not forbidden is compulsory.” In particle physics, this is a useful guide: a process permitted by the relevant conservation laws may occur, although its probability can be extremely small. A process that has not been observed might therefore be forbidden—or simply too rare for experiments to have detected it.</para>

edits.before: <para id="import-auto-id1169737784242">There are hundreds of particles, all hadrons, not listed in <link target-id="import-auto-id1169736657305"/>, most of which have shorter lifetimes. The systematics of those particle lifetimes, their production probabilities, and decay products are completely consistent with the conservation laws noted for lepton families, baryon number, and strangeness, but they also imply other quantum numbers and conservation laws. There are a finite, and in fact relatively small, number of these conserved quantities, however, implying a finite set of substructures. Additionally, some of these short-lived particles resemble the excited states of other particles, implying an internal structure. All of this jigsaw puzzle can be tied together and explained relatively simply by the existence of fundamental substructures. Leptons seem to be fundamental structures. Hadrons seem to have a substructure called quarks. We have so far discovered six quarks in three generations: up and down quarks, charm and strange quarks, and top and bottom quarks.</para>
